content: The coccyx, also known as the tailbone, is the terminal segment of the human vertebral column. It consists of four fused vertebrae, referred to as the coccygeal vertebrae, located inferior to the sacrum. The coccyx is connected to the sacrum via a fibrocartilaginous joint, which allows for limited movement between the two structures. The term coccyx is derived from the Greek word for cuckoo, as its shape resembles the beak of a cuckoo bird. The coccyx serves as an attachment site for nine muscles, including the gluteus maximus and muscles involved in defecation. It also functions as a shock absorber when an individual sits, although excessive force or impact can result in injury and subsequent pain. In species with tails, the coccygeal vertebrae support the tail and accommodate its associated nerves. Structurally, the coccyx is typically composed of four rudimentary vertebrae, though the number can range from three to five. It articulates superiorly with the sacrum. The first three segments of the coccyx may exhibit rudimentary bodies, as well as articular and transverse processes, while the final segment (or sometimes the third) is merely a small nodule of bone. None of the coccygeal segments possess pedicles, laminae, or spinous processes. The first segment is the largest and resembles the lowest sacral vertebra, often existing as a separate piece, while the remaining segments decrease in size from superior to inferior. Contrary to common anatomical descriptions, the coccyx is not always fused in adults. Studies have shown that the coccyx may consist of up to five separate bony segments, with the most common configuration being two or three segments. Only about 5% of the population has a coccyx that is fully fused into one piece, separate from the sacrum, as described in many anatomy textbooks. This misconception can lead to misdiagnoses, such as labeling a segmented coccyx on an X-ray as a fractured coccyx. The anterior surface of the coccyx is slightly concave and features three transverse grooves that mark the junctions between its segments. This surface provides attachment for the anterior sacrococcygeal ligament and the levator ani muscles, and it supports part of the rectum. The posterior surface is convex and also marked by transverse grooves. It presents a linear row of tubercles on either side, which are the rudimentary articular processes of the coccygeal vertebrae. The superior pair of these tubercles, known as the coccygeal cornua, are larger and articulate with the sacral cornua, completing the foramen for the posterior division of the fifth sacral nerve. The lateral borders of the coccyx are thin and exhibit small eminences that represent the transverse processes of the coccygeal vertebrae. The first transverse process is the largest, flattened anteroposteriorly, and often ascends to join the lower part of the lateral edge of the sacrum, completing the foramen for the anterior division of the fifth sacral nerve. The remaining transverse processes diminish in size from superior to inferior and are often absent. The borders of the coccyx provide attachment for the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments, the coccygeus muscle anterior to the ligaments, and the gluteus maximus posterior to them. The apex of the coccyx is rounded and serves as the attachment site for the tendon of the external anal sphincter (sphincter ani externus). In some cases, the apex may be bifid. The sacrococcygeal and intercoccygeal joints are variable in nature and may present as synovial joints, thin fibrocartilaginous discs, intermediate forms between these two, or as ossified structures. Injury to the coccyx can result in a condition known as coccydynia, characterized by pain in the region of the tailbone. Additional anatomical images often depict the vertebral column, the levator ani muscle from within, and median sagittal sections of the male and female pelvis for further context.
